entries.title: DiVR: New Evaluation of Learned Block Regeneration for Diffusion Language Models
summary: The new DiVR study evaluates using learned outcome scores to decide when a diffusion language model should regenerate a whole block, keeping the generator unchanged.

Its controlled comparisons show how targeted revision can improve average reasoning accuracy with fewer forward passes than the tested search baselines, while documenting limits in calibration and repair reliability.

evidence.rationale: The complete22-page primary was read, including diagnostic methods, all matched results and AppendicesA-G; sourceTable1 and calibrationTable9 images inspected. This selection concerns newly disclosed scientific evidence for an existing implementation: the November11 initial repository already contains the verifier, guided decoder, SFT recipe and baselines, while its complete33-entry tree/README has no manuscript, result tables, Sudoku diagnosis or calibration study. The November13 repository diff only adds the paper link/citation and is not itself a research update. The newly announced manuscript supplies the controlled diagnosis and measured comparisons: its frozen-backbone LoRA/head verifier pools masked and visible response positions, learns outcome classification plus within-question ranking, and selectively regenerates32-token blocks with four alternatives/at mostthree events. With the same SFT LLaDA-8B generator, the authors report five-benchmark unweighted accuracy35.3→43.4%; cost1.9–3.5times paired greedy counts row-weighted forwards including verification. Same-loop signal controls and fixed-candidate selection separate verifier quality from extra search. Original cs.CL FridayNovember13 batch plus official Thursday20:00EST schedule imply November13 01:00UTC manuscript availability; retain November12 receipt and actual earliest catalog discoveryNovember13 11:05:43.728UTC. This is delayed review inside the72-hour lookback, not a new Sunday method/code release.
evidence.limitations: Older code/settings alone do not establish earlier public manuscript evidence, but the checked history is a bounded absence search rather than proof of first-ever publication. Costs are forward counts, not latency, FLOPs or total verifier-training expense. Only7B/8B masked-diffusion generators and five math/code benchmarks were tested; code uses MBPP-visible grader tests, and the SFT HumanEval gain is only0.6points. Search baselines are local reimplementations, and Prism answer-selection variants differ. A failed rollout label is not a token-error label; raw class-balanced scores are not calibrated success probabilities. Post-hoc calibration preserves ranking and is not credited with main accuracy gains; its one-event paired intervention does not validate the adaptive three-event policy. The Sudoku diagnosis uses tiny4x4 puzzles. Guidance also breaks some correct answers; seed checks vary one component rather than independently repeating the whole pipeline. No released trained verifier weights or independent reproduction was verified.

entries.title: CoLFA: Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: CoLFA organizes failed multi-agent traces around handoffs and shared content, selecting related decisions and replacing repeated text with references before one attribution call.
Its newly available full study reports more accurate error localization with fewer attribution tokens on Who&When and LongRCA, making the design useful for cheaper debugging of long execution logs.
The gains concern retrospective diagnosis, with repair effectiveness untested and smaller-benchmark confidence intervals crossing zero.

evidence.rationale: Complete 23-page v1 read: main methods/results and Appendices A-G, including exact selection rules, baseline adaptations, token accounting, paired bootstrap and matched-step controls. Primary Tables 1-3 on PDF page 7 and Table 10 on page 20 were also viewed as rendered images. The output agent retains all decision steps; a selected upstream agent is expanded through content correspondence, with one-hop supply records from other agents. A trace overview, content references and original step indices support one LLM attribution call. Evaluation uses all 184 failed Who&When traces and 1,140 LongRCA traces. With two main backbones, exact localization improves by 1.84-3.26 percentage points over each setting's most accurate baseline while attribution token use drops by 66-90%; Claude Sonnet 5.5 supplies a smaller third-backbone comparison on Who&When. These are newly inspectable quantitative results, bootstrap analysis and controls, not a claim that the mechanism was first disclosed today: the identical November 8 README already described it and asserted unquantified ranking claims. The repository currently contains only README and gitignore, with a November 12 metadata-only commit. Original November 11 03:38:54 UTC submission is retained; the native original cs.CL Friday November 13 batch and official 20:00 EST announcement schedule support inferred November 13 01:00 UTC public availability. This is delayed November 15 scientific selection of an item cataloged November 13, preserving that actual first_seen.
evidence.limitations: Retrospective benchmark labels are not direct causal validation of repairs or subsequent task success. Rules assume recorded handoffs, recognizable content and known delegation or broadcast configurations; restricting candidate steps can omit the true error. Who&When supplies task reference answers whereas LongRCA does not. LongRCA includes 108 single-agent traces and is dominated by 685 TravelPlanner traces. Trace-level paired 10,000-replicate bootstrap intervals are positive on LongRCA but cross zero on Who&When; no independent training-seed or deployment study is established. ECHO and RAFFLES were author reimplementations, and token totals exclude embedding requests, CPU preprocessing, latency and monetary pricing. A public README is verified, but implementation and per-trace outputs are not yet released; no code link or independent reproduction is claimed. Abstract maxima compare against individual weak baselines and are not used as the headline.

entries.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
summary: CapLite commits write operations before reading tool results and uses deterministic schema rules to admit sensitive arguments only when grounded in the user request.
This separates a small model's proposals from authorization: the authors report no successful tool-goal attacks in 13,935 AgentDojo episodes across 15 models.
The protection trades away task utility and leaves final answers and free-text payloads unprotected, so it is a scoped write-control design rather than complete prompt-injection immunity.

evidence.rationale: Complete 19-page v1 read, including all main methods/results, Appendices A-H, baseline ports, model tables, benign-failure analysis, grounding implementation and all five recorded case studies. Primary Tables 1-2 on PDF page 6 were directly viewed. A request-only Planner commits at most ten calls before observations; a read-only Reader, candidate-selecting Binder and payload Composer propose arguments, while deterministic mediation enforces a prefix of committed writes and exact membership in the request grounding set for schema-derived authority fields. The main experiment uses 15 open models, including 13 models of 1.7B-12B, with fixed seed and temperature zero. The main attack denominator is 15 times 929 tool-goal pairs, yielding 0/13,935; utility under attack uses all 949 pairs per model. Authors report 29.0% attacked utility versus 27.2% for their CaMeL port, with 17.1K versus 93.7K prompt-plus-completion tokens per episode, averaged across 97 benign and 949 attacked episodes. Eight-model robustness tests add tool-knowledge, read-exfiltration and descriptor-collision attacks; mediator and write-commitment ablations admit attacks. Original November 12 17:07:22 UTC receipt is preserved; the original cs.AI Friday November 13 batch and official EST announcement schedule support inferred November 13 01:00 UTC availability. Delayed selection retains the actual November 13 catalog first_seen rather than inventing a Sunday release. No older complete public artifact was established by the primary links and bounded title/repository searches.
evidence.limitations: Write integrity is relative to trusted requests, tools, documentation, deterministic field classification and canonicalized grounding. Payload text, temporal/control values and final answers are not generally protected; 20 answer-only injection pairs are excluded from the ASR denominator, and the paper shows CapLite repeating an injected final-answer sentence. A value appearing in the request is not proof that the selected operation is semantically correct. Benign/attacked utility is 28.1%/29.0%, versus 59.4%/50.2% undefended; unknown identifiers require confirmation, which the main evaluation does not answer. Schema heuristics classify 17 human-labeled authority arguments as temporal/control, so semantic protection beyond the defined authority class is not established. One benchmark with four suites, one deterministic run per configuration and limited design-aware variants do not establish security against every adaptive attack or deployed environment. Ports and an explicit DRIFT parser adjustment matter; token totals are not measured latency or dollar costs. The paper states a code/outcome release, but no matching author implementation URL was verified in the paper, HTML or bounded public repository search; no code or project link is asserted and no source was executed.

entries.title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
summary: SubGPU Pipelining divides a decoding graph into stages on disjoint groups of GPU streaming multiprocessors, then streams microbatches through them to overlap operators with different resource demands.

A one-B200 prototype replaying a GPT-OSS 120B deployment shard reduces decoder iteration time by 10.33%, showing how spatial scheduling can improve memory utilization without rewriting the operator kernels.
The larger throughput-frontier gains are simulation results, rather than measurements from a 32-GPU serving deployment.

evidence.rationale: Complete13-page v1 read, Sections3–7 and Algorithms1–2 including modeling, search, hardware controls and limitations; no appendix exists. Search jointly chooses predecessor-closed contiguous cuts, stage/boundary reuse, even SM allocations and microbatch size using an event-driven shared-resource simulator. Physical proof uses one B200 to replay a per-rank GPT-OSS120B workload representing attentionTP8/DP4 and MoEEP32,32,768-token context, global decode batch2,048, TensorRT-LLM1.3.0rc22.post1. Two Green Contexts allocate68SMs to full attention and80SMs to remaining operators across two layers. After20warmups, three rounds of100uninstrumented CUDA Graph replays reduce36-layer makespan14.970→13.424ms; separate200kHz captures across four steady replays raise mean DRAM throughput71.8→83.6%of peak while activeSM throughput falls85.9→71.7%. Up-to2.2xper-user/1.9xper-GPU frontier gains are explicitly modeled. This delayed review preserves earliest successful team discovery November13 11:09:02.287458UTC from the pinned primaryDCindex; original receipt is November11 01:51:44UTC. The native primaryDC NEW FridayNovember13 section, plus official November11 holiday and20:00EST release schedule, supports inferred first announcement November13 01:00UTC, inside the72-hour lookback. No earlier full author release was located in the checked primary/search sources.
evidence.limitations: The physical experiment emulates a32-GPU per-rank workload on oneGPU; communication uses virtual endpoint kernels floored at3microseconds plus payload/900GB/s, not a live network. It is a fixed batch/context decoder replay, not an end-to-end serving, quality or latency-SLO measurement. Simulation assumes linear SM compute scaling, calibrated shared-bandwidth/cache policies and negligible stage handoff; its searched frontiers are neither measured outcomes nor a proof of global optimality. Hardware allocation is separately tuned, not directly predicted by the model. Gains can disappear with small batches, compute-heavy kernels or L2working-set pressure; dynamic allocation, persistent workers, weight prefetch and recovery remain future work. No matching released author implementation or independent reproduction verified.

entries.title: Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels
summary: This Helion study uses compiler intermediate representation and approximate resource-liveness analysis to choose kernel configurations without running an autotuning search.

On the tested H100 reductions, its default configurations reach 1.27 times the speed of vLLM handwritten kernels and approach fully tuned Helion performance, making useful execution speed available before a costly search.
The report also shows that heuristic seeds mainly improve the early search, with much smaller benefits near the final best configuration.

evidence.rationale: Complete dated primary article read, including family dispatch, live register/shared/tensor-memory estimates, occupancy and spill constraints, multi-matmul conflict ranking, reduction persistence, all benchmarks and seed-search controls. The H100 study reports1.18xforward and1.12xforward-plus-backward over FLA across96linear-attention kernel/shape cells;153cells across six vLLM reductions reach1.27xCUDA/C++ versus1.31xfull Helion autotuning. General suites cover80reduction and70matmul cells; fusion differences qualify the matmul baseline. A38-kernel paired seed experiment counts failures and reports median103.5→2.5configs to get within25%of best, but255.5→175within5%and521.5→420.5for completion; replayed final winners differ by less than a percent. Scientific novelty here is the newly dated methodology/evaluation disclosure of an existing implementation, not a newly released compiler: inspected source history extends at least October8 and current initialization verifies eligibility/fallback/default promotion mechanics without executing code. Preserve earliest successful prior index discovery November13 11:09:02.735726UTC. Primary article published_time/datePublished metadata agree on November12 16:45:26UTC, which lies after this run's November12 11:00UTC lookback boundary.
evidence.limitations: Kernel benchmarks are not full-model inference or training speedups. Resource placement is predicted rather than measured from Triton output, runtime-unknown extents fall back to the old default, and heuristic constants were tuned for H100/B200 Triton; broader backend portability is not demonstrated. HSTU jagged attention regresses versus the old default, and some matmul comparisons include different intermediate materialization/fusion. Search counts include failed configs and are not wall-clock tuning-time ratios. Seeded and unseeded searches reach similar final quality; no independent reproduction, complete benchmark-run variance table or claim that static analysis beats full search.
